## "They sent it. Now what?"

Your Quality Analyst (QA) forwards the email without comment beyond the subject line: "Attached
per your request." Attached is a PDF, 80-odd pages, watermarked, with a cover letter from an
accounting firm you've never heard of and a title that reads, in full, something like
*"Independent Service Auditor's Report on [Vendor]'s Description of Its System and the Suitability
of the Design and Operating Effectiveness of Controls."* This is the device-management platform
vendor's SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) report — the first time anyone at Lakeshore
has ever actually asked for it, let alone read it.

You asked for it because last module finally did the thing nobody had done before: it tiered this
vendor High. High tier, per the scheme you just built, means a real qualification file — and a
real qualification file means the vendor's own assurance evidence stops being a line item
("yes, they have one") and starts being something you and your QA actually read.

She's already flipping through it, and she asks the two questions everyone asks the first time
they open one of these: "Is this good? And does it tell us anything about what happened with the
Brookfield laptop?" Both are fair questions. Neither has a one-word answer, and getting to the
real answer is this module's entire job.

## Why this matters, and the ITSM bridge

Name the failure mode this report exists to prevent, because it's not "vendors sometimes have bad
security." It's narrower and more common: an organization takes a vendor's own word for its
security posture — a sales deck, a checkbox on a procurement form, a line in a contract that says
"vendor maintains industry-standard safeguards" — and never independently checks whether any of
that is actually tested by anyone who isn't the vendor itself. A SOC 2 report exists specifically
to break that cycle: it's produced by an independent accounting firm, not the vendor's own
marketing team, and it says, in writing, exactly what was tested, over what period, and what the
auditor actually found — including what it didn't find, or couldn't verify.

You already know this shape of control from the generic IT-compliance world: a SOX (Sarbanes-Oxley)
-style vendor attestation, or a third-party risk questionnaire that asks a vendor to produce its
own independent audit evidence instead of a self-reported security survey. SOC 2 is the
general-purpose, cross-industry version of exactly that idea, run by the accounting profession
rather than any blood-industry body. The reason it matters *here*, specifically, is the same
reason module 1 built a tiering scheme in the first place: a High-tier vendor is one whose own
failure could put e-PHI (electronic protected health information) at risk or disrupt a process an
AABB (Association for the Advancement of Blood & Biotherapies) assessor would ask about. For a
vendor at that tier, "they say their security is fine" isn't evidence. An independently tested
report is the closest thing to evidence Lakeshore is going to get without auditing the vendor
itself — which Lakeshore has neither the standing nor the resources to do.

One honest note before you go further, because it sets up everything else in this module: **SOC 2
is not a government regulation, not an AABB Standard, and not something FDA inspects Lakeshore
against directly.** It's a paid, proprietary framework published by the AICPA (American Institute
of Certified Public Accountants) — the accounting profession's own standard-setting body, not a
healthcare or blood-industry regulator. Nothing in this lesson quotes AICPA's own text, because
this curriculum has never purchased or independently read it, the same honest limitation this
curriculum has already applied to ISO 31000, ISO 19011, and GAMP 5 (Good Automated Manufacturing
Practice) elsewhere. What follows is the real, publicly well-known *structure* of a SOC 2 report —
described in this course's own words, not cited to a section or paragraph number, because no such
citation exists in verified form for this curriculum to give you.

## The rule in plain English

Strip away the jargon and a SOC 2 report answers four questions, every time, in roughly this
order:

1. **Point in time, or over time?** Did an auditor check that the vendor's controls are *designed*
   reasonably (Type I), or did the auditor actually watch those controls *operate* for months and
   confirm they worked the whole time (Type II)? These are very different claims, and conflating
   them is the single most common mistake a reader makes.
2. **Which categories of control did the vendor choose to be tested on?** A SOC 2 report is scoped
   — the vendor picks which Trust Services Criteria (TSC) its own report covers, and a report that
   covers only one category says nothing at all about the others.
3. **What does the report say is the customer's own job?** Buried, usually near the back, is a
   section listing the controls the report assumes *Lakeshore* — not the vendor — is responsible
   for implementing. Skip this section and you've only read half the report.
4. **How current is it, right now?** A Type II report covers a past window of months. If Lakeshore
   is reading it well after that window closed, the report is, strictly, already out of date for
   anything that's happened since.

Apply that to your QA's two questions. "Is this good?" depends entirely on how the vendor answered
questions 1 and 2 — a Type II report covering the right categories is strong evidence; a Type I
report covering only one category is a much thinner claim, even if it's the exact same vendor.
"Does it tell us anything about Brookfield?" depends on questions 3 and 4 — and, as this module
gets to honestly, the real answer is more interesting than either a flat yes or no.

## Citation decoder

There's one entry in this table, and — same as this curriculum's handling of ISO 31000, ISO 19011,
and GAMP 5 — it names a framework, not a citable passage.

| Citation | How to read it aloud | What it requires | In our scenario |
|---|---|---|---|
| SOC 2 (AICPA, Trust Services Criteria) | "S-O-C two" — not a numbered regulation or Standard | **Industry practice / proprietary framework — described in this curriculum's own words, not a cited standard.** AICPA's own report format and criteria language are paid, proprietary material never independently fetched or quoted here. What's described below are the framework's real, publicly well-known structural features (report types, criteria categories, CUECs, bridge letters) — never a verbatim sentence, section number, or paragraph attributed to AICPA. | The device-management platform vendor's own report, read for its structure, not quoted for its wording. |

## The actual text — and why there isn't any to quote

Be precise about what backs this module, the same discipline the last module applied to AABB's QSE
4. AICPA's own report language, its exact Trust Services Criteria wording, and the detailed
"points of focus" under each criterion are copyrighted, paid material. This curriculum has never
purchased, fetched, or quoted any of it, and nothing below should be read as a paraphrase close
enough to stand in for the real text.

What *can* be stated confidently, because it's real, publicly well-known, and independent of
AICPA's own copyrighted wording:

- **Type I** reports assess whether a vendor's controls are *suitably designed* as of a single
  point in time — a snapshot of the blueprint, not evidence the blueprint was followed.
- **Type II** reports assess whether those same controls *actually operated effectively* over a
  review period, typically six to twelve months — materially stronger assurance, because it's
  evidence of sustained operation, not just a design that looked good on paper the day it was
  drawn up.
- There are **five Trust Services Criteria**: **Security** (the only one every SOC 2 report must
  include — sometimes called the "common criteria," since every other category builds on top of
  it), **Availability**, **Processing Integrity**, **Confidentiality**, and **Privacy**. A vendor
  selects which of the latter four apply to its own report's scope, based on what it wants
  assessed. A report scoped to Security alone says literally nothing, one way or the other, about
  that same vendor's Availability or Confidentiality controls — scope silence isn't evidence of
  absence, but it isn't evidence of presence either.
- A real SOC 2 report includes a section on **Complementary User Entity Controls (CUECs)** —
  controls the report explicitly states the *customer* is expected to have in place for the
  vendor's own controls to work as described. This section is real, frequently present, and
  frequently skipped by readers who stop at the auditor's opinion letter and never reach it.
- A **bridge letter** is the vendor's own interim attestation — not a new audit — covering the gap
  between a Type II report's period-end date and whatever later date a customer is actually relying
  on the report for. Because a Type II report is inherently backward-looking, a customer reading it
  months after the period closed has no independent evidence that nothing material changed in the
  meantime, unless the vendor provides one.

None of that is AICPA's exact language. It's this curriculum's own description of features any
competent reader would recognize in a real report, held deliberately at arm's length from anything
resembling a citation.

## Reading the device-management platform vendor's report

Here's the actual exercise: walk the same four questions from "the rule in plain English," applied
to a specific, high-stakes vendor, and reason through each answer instead of asserting it.

**Which Trust Services Criteria did it plausibly select?** Security, almost certainly — no SOC 2
report exists without it, and a vendor managing enrollment, policy push, and remote lock-and-wipe
across every device at every site Lakeshore operates is squarely a security-relevant service by
any definition. Availability is the next strong, reasoned guess, not a coin flip: this platform's
entire value proposition depends on being reachable — enrollment has to work, policy pushes have
to land, and a remote wipe command (the one module 1's `investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident`
confirmed was *issued* but never confirmed *delivered*, because the Brookfield laptop never came
back online) only matters if the platform itself is up when it's needed. A vendor selling exactly
that kind of always-on management service has every commercial reason to have its Availability
controls tested and to say so. Confidentiality is the closer call, and worth reasoning through
rather than assuming: this platform handles enrollment records, telemetry, and account data for
devices that — per this course's own locked facts — carry e-PHI-adjacent extracts off-site. A
vendor serving healthcare and blood-industry customers at this scale has a real business reason to
have Confidentiality tested too, even though its core function is device management, not data
processing in the way a transaction system would be. Processing Integrity (accuracy and
completeness of data processing) is the least likely of the remaining three — this platform isn't
performing calculations or transformations on data the way a billing or lab-results system would —
and Privacy (handling of personal information as the vendor's own data-collection activity) is also
a less obvious fit for a device-management function specifically, though not impossible. The
honest, defensible read: **Security and Availability almost certainly in scope, Confidentiality
plausibly in scope given the data this platform's devices carry, Processing Integrity and Privacy
less likely** — and the only way to know for certain is to read the report's own stated scope
section, not guess from the vendor's product category.

**Type I or Type II?** Lean Type II, and say why instead of just asserting it. A vendor mature
enough to serve multiple regulated healthcare and blood-industry customers, at the scale this one
operates, most plausibly maintains an annual Type II report as its standard offering — enterprise
customers in regulated industries routinely require operating-effectiveness evidence, not just a
design snapshot, before relying on a vendor this deeply embedded in device-level security. More to
the point for Lakeshore specifically: a Type I report would tell you the vendor's controls were
*designed* to look reasonable on one date. It would tell you nothing about whether those controls
*actually held up* through something like a platform migration — which is exactly the kind of event
sitting at the center of the unresolved Brookfield question. A Type II report, covering six to
twelve months of actual operation, is the only version of this document that could plausibly speak
to how the vendor's own controls performed across a period that included a migration event. For a
High-tier vendor, read the Type I/Type II line on the cover page first, every time — it changes
what everything after it is actually worth.

**What would the CUEC section plausibly say?** This is where the report earns its place in the
vendor file, and where this module's honesty matters most. A device-management platform's CUEC
section would plausibly include something close to: *the customer is responsible for configuring
and enforcing its own device-enrollment and encryption policies, and for confirming encryption
status on each device before it is placed into field or travel use.* Read that next to what
`investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident` already found, carefully and without rewriting any of
it: that course's own final root-cause ranking named a deployment-sequencing gap — a newly
enrolled device leaving the building before its first encryption attestation had completed — as
the most structural, most likely-to-recur gap behind the Brookfield incident, ahead of the
physical-handling gap and the minimum-necessary gap. That same course was equally clear that the
device-management platform vendor did not fail to secure the device; the vendor's own migration
defect was a known, disclosed issue class the vendor confirmed when asked, not a hidden failure,
and Lakeshore's own *verification* of this one device's encryption status — not the vendor's
control over it — was the actual compliance gap. A CUEC section stating that encryption-status
confirmation is the customer's job is not a surprising footnote. It's exactly the sentence that
would have told Lakeshore, in writing, before any incident, that "confirm the device is actually
encrypted before it travels" was never the vendor's responsibility to guarantee. Reading this
report today doesn't change anything `investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident` already locked. It
does show, honestly, where that same finding would have been sitting in plain sight if anyone had
read this document a year earlier.

**Does Lakeshore need a bridge letter?** Reason through the dates rather than assuming either way.
A Type II report's period end is, by definition, in the past by the time the report is issued and
delivered — commonly a matter of weeks after the period closes — and the report is then typically
relied on for up to a year, until the next one is issued. Lakeshore is reading this report for the
first time, well after the vendor's own review period closed, as part of building a File that
didn't exist until this course started. That gap — between "what this report actually tested" and
"today" — is precisely what a bridge letter exists to cover. The honest answer here isn't "yes" or
"no" in the abstract; it's: **check the report's stated period-end date against today's date, and
if there's a meaningful gap (which, given how this file came together, there almost certainly is),
request a bridge letter now, and build a standing request for one into the annual review of this
vendor's file going forward** — not just once, but every time Lakeshore leans on a report that's
aging past its own tested window, especially after any event (a platform migration, for instance)
that could plausibly have changed something the original report never saw.

**What this report would and would not have told Lakeshore about Brookfield.** Say this plainly,
because it's the honest center of the whole exercise. A SOC 2 report — even a strong, Type II,
properly scoped one — was never going to tell Lakeshore the actual encryption status of one
specific laptop on one specific day. That's a level of device-by-device granularity no
organization-wide assurance report is built to provide; `investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident`
already established that question is, and will likely remain, permanently unresolved, and nothing
in this module reopens that. What a SOC 2 report's CUEC section plausibly *would* have told
Lakeshore, read before the incident instead of after it, is that confirming a device's encryption
status before it leaves controlled use was never the vendor's job to do for Lakeshore — it was
Lakeshore's own control to run. That's not a smaller finding than "the report would have prevented
the incident." It's a different, more useful one: a genuine teaching moment about reading a vendor's
own assurance report *before* an incident forces the question, not instead of fixing the actual
process gap the investigation already found.

## What an auditor — or your own internal reviewer — would actually look for

Nobody from AICPA inspects Lakeshore's vendor file. The people who will actually ask about this
report are an AABB assessor reviewing the High-tier vendor file module 1 just justified, or your
own CIO asking what "we read their SOC 2" actually means in practice. What they'd want to see,
concretely: the report itself, dated; a note of which Type (I or II) it is and the period it
covers; a short, written record of which Trust Services Criteria it includes — not just "we
checked, it's fine"; a note confirming someone actually read the CUEC section and can name what it
requires of Lakeshore; and, if the report's period-end date is more than a few months behind
today, either a bridge letter on file or a documented decision to request one. A weak answer sounds
like "yes, they sent us a SOC 2 report, it's in the folder." A credible answer sounds like
everything this module just walked through, written down, with a name and a date attached.

## Common traps

**"They have a SOC 2 report, so their security is covered."** Covered for *what*, exactly? A report
scoped to Security alone says nothing about Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity, or
Privacy — "they have a SOC 2" is not a complete sentence until you've named which criteria the
report actually includes. A vendor can hold a perfectly real SOC 2 report and still have never been
tested on the exact category a reader assumed it covered.

**"Type I and Type II are basically the same thing, just a formality."** They are not even close to
the same claim. Type I is a design snapshot on one date; Type II is evidence of sustained operation
across months. A vendor whose controls look good on paper but have never been tested in operation
is exactly the gap Type II exists to close — treating the two as interchangeable is one of the
fastest ways to overstate how much assurance a report actually gives.

## What this means for your job

- **Never accept "they have a SOC 2" without asking which type and which criteria.** Those two
  facts, sitting on the report's own cover page and scope section, change what the document is
  actually worth — ask for them by name, every time, for every High-tier vendor.
- **Read the CUEC section yourself, or have your QA do it and report back specifically.** It's the
  section most readers skip, and it's the one most likely to tell you what Lakeshore's own job is —
  which is exactly the kind of finding a deployment-sequencing gap like Brookfield's hides inside.
- **Check the report's period-end date against today, every time you rely on it.** A Type II
  report doesn't stay current forever; if there's a real gap, that's a bridge letter request, not
  something to let slide because the report "still looks recent enough."
- **Don't let a vendor's assurance report quietly expand to cover questions it was never asked.** A
  Security-and-Availability report doesn't tell you anything about Confidentiality just because the
  vendor feels trustworthy — if a specific concern matters to Lakeshore, confirm it's actually in
  the report's own scope, not assumed into it.
- **Treat "we read their SOC 2 report" as a dated, attributable action, not a box on a checklist.**
  The same discipline this course applied to tiering decisions applies here: a credible vendor file
  shows who read it, when, and what they found — not just that a PDF exists somewhere.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q1: Your QA asks, "The vendor's SOC 2 report covers Security and Availability. Does that mean we can also tell our CIO their Confidentiality controls are solid?"

No — and this is worth being precise about rather than letting the good news about Security and
Availability bleed into a category the report never actually tested. A report scoped to Security
and Availability says nothing, one way or the other, about Confidentiality. If Confidentiality
matters for this vendor relationship (and given the e-PHI-adjacent data its managed devices carry,
it plausibly does), the honest answer is "unknown — ask the vendor whether a Confidentiality-scoped
report exists, or will exist at the next renewal," not an assumption borrowed from an adjacent
category that happened to test well.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q2: Does the SOC 2 report's own text establish, in a way this curriculum could cite to an assessor, the exact Trust Services Criteria wording or a specific AICPA section number?

No, and this is deliberate. SOC 2's actual report language and the detailed Trust Services Criteria
"points of focus" are AICPA's own paid, proprietary material, never independently purchased or
read for this curriculum. What's taught here — Type I/Type II, the five criteria's names, CUECs,
bridge letters — is this course's own description of the framework's real, publicly well-known
structure, the same tier of handling this curriculum already gives ISO 31000, ISO 19011, and GAMP
5. If a specific sentence or section number is ever needed for a real audit, it has to come from
someone who has actually read the current AICPA guidance — not from this lesson.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Q3: If the device-management platform vendor's SOC 2 report had existed and been read a year before the Brookfield incident, would it have told Lakeshore the laptop's encryption status that day?

No — and don't let anyone claim otherwise. `investigating-a-healthcare-data-incident` already
established that this specific device's encryption status is a permanent unknown, for structural
reasons (no attestation ever completed, on either platform, before the device was lost) that no
organization-wide assurance report could have reached into. What an earlier reading of this report
plausibly *would* have surfaced is the CUEC section's statement that confirming a device's
encryption status before travel use is Lakeshore's own job, not the vendor's guarantee — reinforcing
a process gap the investigation found on its own, not resolving the one unresolved fact at the
center of it.
:::

## Where this goes next

The device-management platform vendor's SOC 2 report just told you what it tells you about its
*operations* — tested, independently, over time. It says nothing at all about the *management
system* governing how the vendor chooses and reviews its controls in the first place, or whether
its certification actually covers the specific product Lakeshore uses. That's a different
document, from a different body, with its own structure worth reading just as carefully: next
module opens the vendor's ISO 27001 certificate and Statement of Applicability.
